summary: Students aged 12–13 learn to distinguish two separate human-driven threats to coral reefs that share one root cause (rising CO2 from burning fossil fuels): thermal bleaching (heat stress makes coral expel its symbiotic algae, losing colour and most of its food) and chemical acidification (dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowers pH, reduces carbonate ions, and weakens/dissolves calcium-carbonate skeletons). The core insight is that these are DIFFERENT mechanisms needing different fixes, with reef loss cascading to the ~25% of marine species that depend on reef structure. Activities build from anchoring the coral–algae mutualism, through a two-lever reef model where learners drive temperature and CO2 and observe distinct failures, to argument/evaluation of which interventions address which cause.
misconceptions: 'Bleached coral is dead coral' — bleaching is a stress response; brief bleaching can recover if the algae return, though prolonged bleaching is fatal.
'Coral is a plant' or 'coral bleaches because it loses its own colour' — coral is an animal; most of its colour and food come from the symbiotic algae it expels.
'Bleaching and acidification are the same thing' — one is thermal (heat expels algae), the other chemical (CO2 lowers pH and carbonate); they have different mechanisms and different fixes.
'Acidification means the ocean is turning into acid' — seawater stays slightly alkaline; it is becoming LESS alkaline / more acidic (lower pH), which is enough to reduce carbonate availability.
'Cooling the water or shading reefs would fix everything' — that can relieve bleaching but does nothing for acidification, which only falls with reduced CO2.

activities.title: Drive the reef: two levers, two different failures
steps: Work with a reef model that has two separate controls: water temperature and atmospheric/dissolved CO2.
Raise the TEMPERATURE and describe what happens: zooxanthellae drain out of the polyps, the coral turns white, and a coral food/energy meter falls.
Hold the heat high and observe the coral die; then, in a fresh run, ease the heat back quickly and watch colour return — state in your own words why duration matters, not just peak temperature.

Separately raise the CO2 and describe the different failure: a pH readout falls, carbonate-ion tokens the coral needs to build its skeleton become scarce, growth stalls, and skeleton edges pit and dissolve.
Watch a linked species panel: reef-dependent fish and invertebrates thin out as the reef structure is lost (~25% of marine species).
Test restoration levers (cut emissions, shade/cool the water, plant heat-tolerant coral) and record which lever repairs which failure.

Toggle 'cool the water' after bleaching and acidification have both appeared: note that bleaching recovers — provided the heat stress was not already prolonged to the point of death — while the acidification damage does not budge, and explain what this reveals.
activities.insight: Bleaching is a reversible-until-it-isn't stress response driven by heat, while acidification is a chemical attack on the skeleton driven by CO2; they are two distinct threats from the same emissions, and only cutting CO2 addresses both.

activities.title: Inside the polyp: anatomy and the two mechanisms
steps: Examine a cutaway of a coral polyp and identify the zooxanthellae living inside its tissue; state in your own words that these algae give the coral its colour AND most of its food.

Compare three states side by side — a healthy coloured polyp, a bleached polyp (still a live animal whose transparent tissue reveals the white skeleton beneath after the algae are expelled), and a coral whose skeleton is pitted/dissolving from acidification — and say which threat produced each.
Follow a labelled chemistry chain and fill in the missing steps: CO2 + H2O → carbonic acid (H2CO3) → lower pH → fewer carbonate ions → harder to build/maintain the CaCO3 skeleton.
Write a one-sentence contrast: how the thermal mechanism differs from the chemical mechanism.
activities.insight: The coral is an animal in mutualism with photosynthetic algae; losing those algae starves it and reveals the white skeleton through its still-living tissue (bleaching), while a separate chemistry chain (CO2→carbonic acid→↓pH→↓carbonate) physically weakens its skeleton (acidification).

activities.title: Does acid attack something hard? Predict–Observe–Explain
steps: Before observing, write a prediction with a reason: could a weak acid damage something as hard as a seashell or coral skeleton? Most people expect 'no, it's too hard'.

Observe a clean shell or a piece of natural chalk or limestone (calcium carbonate) placed in vinegar; note the immediate fizzing (carbon dioxide gas being released) as the surface is attacked and slowly dissolves. Note: many blackboard chalks are calcium sulfate and will not fizz, so check the material first.
Explain the link to ocean acidification: CO2 makes seawater more acidic, attacking the same calcium carbonate that corals and shellfish build.

State the important caveat in your own words: vinegar is far stronger than seawater, so the ocean effect is much slower and gentler. The shared chemistry is that acid reacts with carbonate, but in the ocean this mainly lowers the number of carbonate ions, making skeletons harder to build and easier to wear away, rather than visibly fizzing them away. Seawater stays slightly alkaline and becomes LESS alkaline, not an actual acid.
activities.insight: Hard calcium-carbonate structures are not safe from acids; a mildly more acidic ocean is enough to reduce carbonate availability and attack skeletons over time.

activities.title: Interview a reef scientist: trade-offs and evaluation
steps: Interview (in role-play or with a knowledgeable persona) a marine biologist who has surveyed a bleaching event; ask what they saw and why some reefs recover while others do not.
Pose the evaluation questions: is restoration worth it? Should effort go to cutting emissions or to engineering heat-tolerant coral? What has already been lost?
Argue, using the two-mechanism model, why local fixes such as shade, cooling, or restoration help bleaching but cannot solve acidification.
State which interventions target which cause, and why reducing CO2 is the only lever that addresses both.
activities.insight: Evaluating responses requires matching each intervention to the mechanism it affects; because acidification only eases with reduced CO2, local-only measures are insufficient on their own.

activities.title: Sort and sequence: consolidate the two chains
steps: Sequence the acidification chain in order: CO2 → carbonic acid → lower pH → fewer carbonate ions → weak/dissolving skeleton.
Categorise a mix of symptoms and causes as either bleaching (thermal) or acidification (chemical).
Match each intervention to the cause it addresses (e.g. shading/cooling → bleaching only; cutting emissions → both).
Estimate how much of emitted CO2 the ocean absorbs (~25–30%) and connect that to why ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era.
activities.insight: The two threats have distinct causal chains and distinct fixes; placing each step and symptom in the right chain confirms the learner can keep them separate while recognising the shared CO2 root.

activities.title: Fly through a changing reef (optional immersive view)
steps: Take an optional 3D fly-through over a reef transect and scrub time forward under a combined warming-and-acidifying scenario, watching the reef whiten and erode.
Describe the scale and extent of loss across the transect in your own words.

Connect what you see back to the two mechanisms learned elsewhere: the whitening is heat-driven expulsion of algae, while the crumbling/eroding structure reflects CO2-driven weakening of the skeleton.
activities.insight: An immersive fly-through may convey the scale and felt sense of reef loss; because the concept is chemical/physiological rather than spatial, this view is less suited to conveying the underlying mechanisms, which are better reached through the two-lever model and chemistry chain. Treat it as a context/engagement layer rather than the primary teacher of mechanism.

checkQuestion: A bleached reef is bone-white; nearby, other corals are struggling to build their skeletons at all. A student says 'the heat literally bleached the coral white like bleach does to a T-shirt, and the acid problem is a totally separate thing that just happens to be going on too'. Is a bleached coral 'dead and bleached white', and are warming and acidification two unrelated problems? Explain what actually turns the coral white and what the two threats have in common.
checkAnswer: Bleaching isn't a chemical whitening and the coral isn't necessarily dead. Reef-building corals live in mutualistic symbiosis with tiny photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) inside them, which give the coral both colour and most of its food. When water gets too warm, the stressed coral EXPELS the zooxanthellae; without them it loses its colour (you see the white skeleton through clear tissue) and starves — it can recover if conditions ease soon, or die if not. Acidification is a different mechanism: extra CO2 dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid, lowering the pH and making it harder for corals to build (and easier to dissolve) their calcium carbonate skeletons. But the two threats share ONE root cause — rising CO2 from burning fossil fuels drives BOTH the warming that causes bleaching and the acidification that attacks skeletons.
